Propositions 1–2 also require additional support assumptions. An approximation can equal c·p(θ|x) on the posterior support, with c<1, and place its remaining mass outside that support. A proposal restricted to the posterior support then gives zero variance despite an incorrect posterior. Equation (8) implicitly rules out this possibility without stating the necessary restriction.

The evaluation consists entirely of one conjugate Gaussian model whose posterior has a linear mean and fixed isotropic covariance. Mean and MMD improvements therefore do not establish uniformly better posterior approximation in the likelihood-free setting.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the benefit of this particular loss, which is inherited from Schmitt et al. (2024). A key missing baseline is amortized variational inference using the same flow architecture, unlabeled observations, and likelihood-evaluation budget. The VAE described in Appendix F.1 uses a different posterior family and simulated training data. Furthermore, Table 2 evaluates the same 15 countries used for self-consistency training; results on countries excluded from training should be reported separately.

The strongest posterior-accuracy evidence is confined to the simpler known-likelihood problems. Hodgkin–Huxley is assessed through posterior predictive reconstruction, while MNIST is assessed primarily through qualitative images. Neither establishes posterior correctness or uncertainty calibration. Quantitative posterior diagnostics, calibration assessments, and stronger high-dimensional comparisons are missing; Figure 7 also shows substantial posterior standard-deviation bias with a learned likelihood.

The MNIST observation model is insufficiently specified. As described, it applies a fixed deterministic Gaussian blur without stochastic observation noise. This produces a singular conditional distribution rather than the continuous likelihood density assumed by the objective. The manuscript needs to clarify the probabilistic target of the learned likelihood and the interpretation of its nonzero posterior uncertainty.

Table 1 contains an internal reporting inconsistency. It describes means and standard errors of nonnegative absolute errors across countries, but reports entries such as 0.003 ± 0.009 for alpha with M=4. For such observations, the usual standard error cannot exceed their mean. The aggregation, labels, or numerical results require correction before these summaries can be interpreted reliably.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed appendices. The supplied PDF's code URL is blank. Additionally, Appendix G's published alpha_m equation gives approximately 1.2×10^15 at a membrane potential of -65 mV, which appears incompatible with the stated fixed-step Euler integration at 0.01 ms. The simulator equations and implementation need reconciliation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of amortized Bayesian inference: inaccurate posterior approximation on observations poorly represented by simulations. Applying self-consistency to unlabeled target observations is simple, practically motivated, and preserves fast inference after training.

The Gaussian experiments provide useful controlled evidence, with analytic posterior references, ten independent refits, and ablations covering dimensionality, unlabeled sample size, distribution shift, summary networks, and estimated likelihoods. The reported improvements over standard NPE are substantial.

The air-traffic study adds real-data evidence against Stan, and the appendix includes comparisons with online NPE, prior self-consistency training, and a VAE. The neuroscience and image experiments explore broader applicability, and many architecture and training settings are documented.
weaknesses: The strict-properness theory contains substantive errors. Proposition 4 is false: if p(x|θ)=r(x), then p(θ|x)=p(θ), and any normalized, θ-independent likelihood q(x|θ)=s(x) makes the self-consistency ratio constant across θ, even when s differs from r. Likelihood normalization over x does not establish the claimed uniqueness. Propositions 1–2 also need additional support restrictions: q can be proportional to the posterior on its support while placing extra mass outside it, giving zero variance under a proposal restricted to the posterior support.

The claimed absence of an accuracy–robustness trade-off is stronger than the theory supports. Coincident population optima in an unrestricted distribution family do not eliminate trade-offs under finite network capacity, finite data, imperfect summaries, or likelihood approximation. Sensitivity to the SC weight and proposal sampling, together with tests on multimodal posteriors, would help establish practical reliability.

The contribution is primarily the application of an existing SC objective to target observations. The comparisons do not isolate its advantage over other likelihood-based objectives using the same observations. In particular, the VAE baseline is described as trained on simulated pairs and uses a different encoder. A matched flow-based amortized variational baseline, with the same unlabeled data and likelihood access, is an important missing comparison.

The strongest posterior-accuracy evidence is concentrated in the Gaussian and air-traffic examples. Hodgkin–Huxley is evaluated mainly through posterior predictive mean error, which cannot establish posterior distribution accuracy or uncertainty calibration. MNIST provides qualitative images without aggregate reconstruction metrics, posterior-reference comparisons, or calibration measurements. Visually coherent uncertainty maps do not substantiate the claim of well-calibrated inference.

The MNIST observation model is problematic as specified. Appendix I describes a fixed deterministic Gaussian blur without stochastic observation noise, making the conditional likelihood singular rather than an ordinary density of the type modeled by the likelihood flow. The paper needs to specify the stochastic observation model or explain precisely which surrogate posterior is being targeted.

Some reported statistics are inconsistent with their stated definitions. Table 1 describes means and standard errors of absolute errors across countries, but reports values such as 0.003 ± 0.009 for α with M=4. For nonnegative per-country errors, the conventional standard error cannot exceed their mean. The aggregation procedure and affected table entries require clarification or correction before the quantitative evidence can be fully trusted.

Evidence for generalization beyond the unlabeled observations is incomplete. The additional air-traffic baseline comparison uses all 15 evaluation countries for SC training, while results for M=4 and M=8 aggregate training and held-out countries. Separate held-out-country results over repeated splits would better support the central extrapolation claim.

Reproducibility and computational comparisons remain incomplete. The supplied abstract contains no actual code URL, gradient treatment through posterior-generated SC samples is unspecified, and Stan convergence diagnostics are absent. Comparative training costs and likelihood-evaluation counts are also missing; these are particularly relevant for Hodgkin–Huxley, where evaluating the likelihood requires solving the dynamical model.

strengths: The paper addresses an important weakness of amortized Bayesian inference: inaccurate posteriors on observations poorly represented by simulated training data. Applying self-consistency to unlabeled observations is a useful extension that preserves fast inference after training.

The Gaussian experiments show substantial improvements against analytic posteriors, with ten independent refits and ablations covering dimensionality, unlabeled sample size, summary networks, and estimated likelihoods.

The air-traffic study provides encouraging comparisons against Stan. The additional neuron and image experiments demonstrate implementation breadth, and the appendices provide substantial architectural and optimization details.
weaknesses: Proposition 4 is false as stated. If observations are independent of parameters, then p(theta|x)=p(theta). Any normalized likelihood estimate q(x|theta)=r(x) makes the proposed ratio equal to r(x), constant across theta, even when r differs from the true observation distribution. Thus, knowing the posterior does not make this likelihood self-consistency loss strictly proper. Exchanging likelihood and posterior does not preserve the normalization argument.

The theoretical guarantees are overstated. Propositions 1–2 require additional support restrictions: constancy on the true posterior's support does not exclude an approximator assigning probability elsewhere. Furthermore, shared population minimizers do not establish an absence of practical accuracy–robustness trade-offs in finite-capacity networks, nor guarantee generalization beyond the unlabeled training observations.

The underlying self-consistency loss comes from prior work; the principal contribution is applying it to unlabeled observations. The comparisons do not adequately isolate this contribution from generic likelihood-based adaptation. In Appendix F.1, the VAE uses simulated training data and a restricted Gaussian encoder. A stronger control would use the same posterior architecture, unlabeled observations, and likelihood access while optimizing an amortized variational objective.

The larger experiments do not establish posterior accuracy or calibrated uncertainty. Hodgkin–Huxley evaluation measures posterior predictive mean error, which can improve despite incorrect parameter uncertainty. MNIST evaluation is qualitative, without quantitative reconstruction metrics, posterior references, or uncertainty validation. Moreover, Appendix I specifies deterministic Gaussian blur without an observation-noise model, leaving the continuous likelihood being approximated unclear.

Evidence for generalization beyond the unlabeled observations is limited. Table 2 evaluates the same 15 countries used for self-consistency training, while Table 1 combines countries used and unused during training. Separate results for held-out countries and repeated country splits are needed. The Gaussian extrapolation study explores a comparatively narrow family of mean shifts.

Table 1 contains a statistical reporting inconsistency. For example, it reports mean absolute bias 0.003 with standard error 0.009 across 15 countries. For nonnegative per-country errors, the ordinary sample standard error cannot exceed their mean. The aggregation or error-bar definition therefore needs correction or clarification before these quantitative claims can be trusted.

Reproducibility and computational accounting remain incomplete. The supplied manuscript promises code but provides no usable link, and does not specify whether gradients propagate through posterior proposal samples. Comparative training costs and likelihood-evaluation counts are also absent; these matter particularly when evaluating the likelihood requires solving the neuron model.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: improving amortized posterior inference using observations without known parameters. The approach preserves fast inference after training and integrates naturally with existing neural posterior estimators.

The Gaussian experiments provide clear improvements against analytic posteriors, with ten independent refits and useful ablations covering dimensionality, unlabeled-data quantity, summary networks, and estimated likelihoods.

The air-traffic application provides substantive evidence against Stan reference posteriors. For example, Table 1 reports a reduction in the Wasserstein distance for β from 0.161 to 0.054 using eight unlabeled countries. The appendix also includes online-training and prior self-consistency baselines.

The manuscript documents many architectural and optimization choices, separates MNIST adaptation and evaluation images, and acknowledges the identifiability problem when both likelihood and posterior are learned.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims contain errors. Proposition 4 is false: if x and θ are independent, the known posterior equals the prior, and any normalized likelihood q(x|θ)=r(x) makes the self-consistency ratio constant across θ, even when r differs from the true data distribution. Propositions 1–2 also need additional support restrictions: constancy on the true posterior's support does not exclude q assigning probability outside that support. Consequently, the normalization step in Appendix A is not justified as stated.

The methodological novelty is primarily applying the existing self-consistency objective to unlabeled observations. A crucial comparison is missing: the same posterior architecture trained with NPE plus an ELBO/reverse-KL objective on the same unlabeled observations. The Appendix F.1 VAE uses a different architecture and is described as training on simulated data, so it does not isolate the benefit of the proposed objective from access to target observations.

The higher-dimensional experiments do not establish accurate, calibrated posterior inference. Hodgkin–Huxley evaluation measures posterior predictive fit rather than parameter-posterior accuracy; an incorrect or excessively concentrated posterior can still predict observations well. MNIST evaluation is qualitative, without quantitative reconstruction metrics, reference posterior comparisons, or uncertainty-calibration tests. These results support narrower claims than the manuscript's broad assertions about posterior accuracy.

The MNIST statistical model is underspecified. Appendix I describes a fixed, deterministic Gaussian blur without an observation-noise model. As written, the conditional likelihood is singular rather than an ordinary continuous density. The relationship between this simulator, the learned likelihood density, and the posterior targeted by the self-consistency theory therefore needs clarification.

The air-traffic evidence mixes adaptation and generalization. Table 2 evaluates the same 15 countries used in the self-consistency objective. The four- and eight-country experiments aggregate results across all countries without separately reporting unseen-country performance or clearly identifying the adaptation subsets. These evaluations do not cleanly establish generalization beyond the unlabeled observations.

Some quantitative summaries are inconsistent with their stated definitions. Table 1 describes means and standard errors of nonnegative absolute errors, yet includes values such as 0.003 ± 0.009. Under that aggregation, the standard error cannot exceed the mean. The authors should clarify whether they aggregated signed errors, reported standard deviations, or used another calculation, and correct the table accordingly.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence remain incomplete despite the extensive appendix. The supplied PDF contains no code URL after its code-availability statement, does not clearly specify differentiation through the parameter-dependent proposal distribution, and lacks matched training-cost comparisons accounting for the additional likelihood evaluations. These omissions limit assessment of both implementation and computational competitiveness.
